content: 1. Paper-based registers are used for specific health domains, while digitized registers are employed for longitudinal health programs. These include tracking the health benefits and status of migrant populations. Case management logs are also maintained for specific target populations, including migrants. 2. Health worker decision support refers to digital tools that integrate an individual’s health information with the health worker’s knowledge and clinical protocols. These tools assist health workers in making accurate diagnoses and treatment decisions. 3. A person-centered digital tracking and decision-support (DTDS) system is utilized by health workers at the point of care. It maintains a persistent record of health events and encounters, linking to clinical decision-support systems to promote best practices. 4. The DTDS system also connects to reporting and management tools to enhance accountability. It includes all necessary information to detail an individual’s health status and the interventions provided to them. 5. Community health workers and health volunteers can use these systems to calculate aggregate indicators required for reporting, such as monitoring provider performance, stock levels, and system efficiency. 6. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends digital targeted client communication for addressing health issues related to sexual, reproductive, maternal, newborn, and child health. This is contingent on addressing concerns about sensitive content and data privacy. This recommendation is context-specific. 7. WHO also recommends the use of digital decision-support tools accessible via mobile devices for community and facility-based health workers. These tools should be used for tasks already defined within the health worker’s scope of practice. This recommendation is also context-specific. 8. Digital tracking of clients’ health status and services, combined with decision support, is recommended by WHO under specific conditions. These include settings where the health system can support integrated implementation and tasks within the health worker’s defined scope of practice. 9. WHO further recommends combining digital tracking with decision support and targeted client communication. This is recommended only in contexts where the health system can support integrated implementation, tasks are within the health worker’s scope, and data privacy concerns are addressed. 10. WHO supports the digital provision of educational and training content to health workers. This is intended to complement, not replace, traditional methods of delivering continued health education and post-certification training. 11. Digital Adaptation Kits (DAKs) are part of a broader vision for SMART (Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, and Testable) Guidelines. These aim to improve the fidelity and uptake of recommendations within digital systems through a systematic process for transforming guideline development, delivery, and application. 12. DAKs serve as a prerequisite for developing machine-readable guidelines, executable reference software, and advanced analytics for precision health. They provide a structured approach to integrating WHO guidelines into digital systems. 13. The DAK for family planning aims to provide a common language for program managers, software developers, and implementers of digital systems. It ensures adherence to WHO guidelines and facilitates consistency in health content for person-centered digital tracking and decision-support systems. 14. The DAK includes generic workflows, data elements, and decision-support algorithms derived from WHO documents such as the Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use and the Family Planning Global Handbook for Providers. 15. The DAK also addresses technical considerations for self-care interventions from the perspective of health workers promoting these interventions to clients. It includes linkages to related services for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and intimate partner violence, with considerations for adolescents. 16. The outputs of DAKs are intentionally generic and require contextualization to align with local policies and requirements. DAKs have been developed for other health domains, such as antenatal care, HIV, and STIs, and are being expanded to include immunizations, postnatal care, and child health. 17. The DAK comprises eight interlinked components: health interventions and recommendations, generic personas, user scenarios, business processes and workflows, core data elements, decision-support logic, indicators and performance metrics, and high-level functional and non-functional requirements. 18. Each component of the DAK provides a starting point for adaptation to specific contexts. For example, health interventions and recommendations are based on WHO’s Universal Health Coverage essential interventions and related guidelines. 19. Generic personas depict end-users, supervisors, and stakeholders interacting with the digital system. User scenarios describe how these personas interact within workflows, providing greater specificity for system design. 20. Business processes and workflows outline key activities, such as registration, counseling, and referrals, to achieve health program objectives. These workflows can be customized to include additional pathways or entirely new processes. 21. Core data elements are required throughout the workflow and are linked to data dictionaries for interoperability with other standards-based systems. These elements can be translated into local languages and adapted to specific contexts. 22. Indicators and performance metrics are aggregated for decision-making, performance monitoring, and reporting. These are based on the principle of “collect once, use for many purposes” and can be customized to local needs. 23. The DAK provides guidance on system design, including functional and non-functional requirements, to ensure the system meets the needs of end-users and aligns with budgetary constraints. 24. The primary audience for the DAK includes health program managers within ministries of health, who oversee the implementation of clinical practices and policies. Software development teams and private sector implementers can also benefit from the DAK for evidence-based decision-making. 25. The DAK equips business analysts, who act as intermediaries between health content experts and software developers, with the necessary components to develop standards-compliant digital tracking and decision-support systems.
